summary: This memo defines part of the SNMP Management Information Base for managing multiple logical and physical entities handled by a single SNMP agent. It specifies version 4 of the Entity MIB and obsoletes version 3, published as RFC 4133.

plainLanguage.summary: The Entity MIB gives network management programs a standard way to ask a device what is inside it. It lists the physical parts, such as the chassis, the cards and the ports, and the separate functions the device runs, such as a router or a bridge. It also links the two, so a tool can say which part of the hardware runs which function. This is version 4 of the module.

questions: snmp physical and logical entity management
what changed in entity mib version 4
how does snmp describe hardware in a device
subtitle: A standard SNMP view of the hardware and the functions inside one managed device.

tldr.problem: A single SNMP agent often manages several logical entities, such as two bridges or two OSPF areas, and each of them sits on some part of the same physical device. There was no standard way to describe that layout.
tldr.mechanism: The Entity MIB defines SNMP objects for physical components and logical entities, mapping tables that link them, and a containment relation that records which component holds which.
tldr.outcome: This is version 4 of the module. It adds a UUID object, moves the list of hardware classes to IANA, and adds a reduced compliance statement for devices with little memory.

today: RFC 6933 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current definition of version 4 of the Entity MIB. It replaced RFC 4133, which defined version 3.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
RFC 6933 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the MIB, and are generally reached with the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

The objects are defined using the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This module is compliant with SMIv2, which is described in STD 58, RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

The document specifies version 4 of the Entity MIB and obsoletes version 3 of the module, published as RFC 4133.
sections.plainLanguage: This document defines a standard set of readable and writable objects that a network management program can query over SNMP. The objects describe the parts inside a device, such as its chassis, its cards and its ports. This is version 4, which replaces version 3.

sections.title: Why One Agent Can Hold Many Entities
sections.content:
There is a need for a standardized way of representing a single agent that supports multiple instances of one MIB module. The RFC names three cases that already happen: multiple instances of a bridge supported within a single device that has a single agent; multiple repeaters supported by a single agent; and multiple OSPF backbone areas, each operating as part of its own Autonomous System and each identified by the same area identifier, supported inside a single router with one agent.

The single agent implies a relationship that binds these entities. There is an overall physical entity that houses the sum of the things managed by that one agent, so there are multiple logical entities within a single physical entity. Sometimes the overall physical entity contains several smaller physical entities, and each logical entity is associated with one of them. Sometimes the overall physical entity is a compound of several physical entities, such as a stack of stackable hubs.

What is needed is a way to determine exactly which logical entities the agent manages, so a management station can talk to the agent about a particular logical entity. When different logical entities are associated with different physical entities, the same information also tells them apart.
sections.plainLanguage: One network device can run several separate managed functions at once, such as two bridges or two routing areas. This document gives a standard way to describe those functions and to show which piece of hardware each one runs on.

sections.title: Naming Scopes, Logical and Physical Entities
sections.content:
A naming scope represents the set of information that may be accessed through a single SNMP operation. All instances within a naming scope share the same unique identifier space. For SNMPv1 a naming scope is identified by the value of the associated entLogicalCommunity instance. For SNMPv3 the term context is used instead, and the complete definition of an SNMP context is in Section 3.3.1 of RFC 3411.

A logical entity is a managed component that has at most one instantiation of each of a particular set of MIB objects, with its own set of management functions. Examples given are routers, bridges and print servers. A physical entity, or physical component, is an identifiable physical resource within a managed system. Zero or more logical entities may use a physical resource at any given time, and which components an agent reports is an implementation-specific matter. Typical physical resources are communications ports, backplanes, sensors, daughter-cards, power supplies and the overall chassis.

A containment tree is the conceptual sequence of entPhysicalIndex values that uniquely specifies the exact physical location of a component. It is generated by following and recording each entPhysicalContainedIn instance up the tree towards the root until a value of zero is found, meaning no further containment.
sections.plainLanguage: A naming scope is one separate set of management objects that a single SNMP operation can reach. A logical entity is a function the device performs, such as a router. A physical entity is a real part of the device, such as a port. The containment tree records where each part sits inside the chassis.

sections.title: The Five Object Groups
sections.content:
The Entity MIB contains five groups of MIB objects. The entityPhysical group describes the physical entities managed by a single agent. The entityLogical group describes the logical entities managed by a single agent. The entityMapping group describes the associations between physical entities, logical entities, interfaces and non-interface ports. The entityGeneral group describes general system attributes shared by potentially all types of entities. The entityNotifications group contains status indication notifications.

The entityPhysical group holds a single table, entPhysicalTable, with one row per physical entity. It must always contain at least one row for the overall physical entity, whose entPhysicalClass value should be stack(11), chassis(3) or module(9). Each row is indexed by an arbitrary small integer and holds a description and a type of the entity. It can also hold the index number of another row, which expresses a containment relationship between the two. The containment relationships form a strict hierarchy, so recursion is not allowed.

The class of a physical entity comes from the IANAPhysicalClass enumeration, which the RFC defines in a separate module maintained by IANA. Its values run from other(1) to battery(14) and cover chassis, backplane, container, power supply, fan, sensor, module, port, stack, cpu, energyObject and battery.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects are sorted into five groups: hardware, the functions the device runs, the links between them, general information, and notifications. The hardware group is a table with one row per real component. Each row says what the component is and which bigger component holds it.

sections.title: What Version 4 Changes
sections.content:
Over time there may be a need to add new enumerated values to the PhysicalClass textual convention. To allow for such additions without requiring this MIB module to be reissued, a new module called IANA-ENTITY-MIB was created, providing the IANA-maintained textual convention IANAPhysicalClass. The PhysicalClass textual convention was deprecated.

A new MIB object, entPhysicalUUID, was added to the entPhysicalTable. Compared with entPhysicalUris, the new object is read-only and restricted to a fixed size so that only values compliant with RFC 4122 are allowed. The RFC asks implementations of version 3 to keep storing the UUID in entPhysicalUris in URN format as well, so that older software still finds it. That duplication of information exists to enable backward compatibility, and entPhysicalUris allows write access while entPhysicalUUID does not.

Two new compliance statements were created: entity4Compliance for full compliance with version 4, and entity4CRCompliance for devices with constrained resources, such as batteries, which might require only a limited number of objects to be supported, namely entPhysicalClass, entPhysicalName and entPhysicalUUID. A new textual convention, UUIDorZero, was created to represent a Universally Unique Identifier (UUID) with syntax that conforms to RFC 4122, Section 4.1. Defining it as a textual convention allows future reuse in other MIB modules that import it, and it is included in the UUID-TC-MIB module.
sections.plainLanguage: Version 4 makes three changes. It moves the list of hardware kinds into a separate list that IANA can extend without changing this document. It adds one object that carries a globally unique identifier for a component. It adds a second compliance statement for small devices that can support only a few objects.

sections.title: Compliance Statements
sections.content:
The entity4Compliance statement is for SNMP entities that implement the full version 4 of the Entity MIB. Its mandatory groups are entityPhysicalGroup, entityPhysical2Group, entityPhysical3Group, entityGeneralGroup, entityNotificationsGroup and entityPhysical4Group. The entityLogical2Group is not mandatory for agents that model all MIB object instances within a single naming scope. The entityMappingGroup is optional in the same way, but implementation of the entPhysicalContainsTable is mandatory for all agents, and the entAliasMappingTable can only be supported by an agent that also implements the entityLogicalGroup or the entityLogical2Group.

Some objects have a relaxed minimum access. An agent that cannot identify serial numbers and cannot provide non-volatile storage for management-station-assigned values may make entPhysicalSerialNum not accessible. Write access to entPhysicalAlias is required only if the associated entPhysicalClass value is chassis(3). Write access to entPhysicalAssetID is not required for physical entities whose associated entPhysicalIsFRU value is false(2).

The entity4CRCompliance statement is for SNMP entities that implement version 4 of the Entity MIB on devices with constrained resources. Its mandatory groups are entityPhysicalCRGroup, which collects entPhysicalClass and entPhysicalName, and entityPhysical4Group, which collects entPhysicalUUID.
sections.plainLanguage: The document defines two levels of compliance. Full compliance means an agent supports six groups of objects. The reduced level, meant for small devices, means it supports the class of a component, its name and its unique identifier. Some write access is optional when the device cannot store the values.

sections.title: A Router With Two Slots
sections.content:
The first worked example is a router containing two slots. Each slot contains a 3-port router or bridge module, and each port is represented in the ifTable. There are two logical instances of OSPF running and two logical bridges.

The physical rows follow the hardware. Row 1 is the field-replaceable chassis, with entPhysicalContainedIn set to 0, entPhysicalClass chassis(3), the name '100-A' and the URI 'URN:CLEI:CNME120ARA'. Rows 2 and 3 are the two slots, each a container(5) contained in row 1. Row 4 is the module in slot 1, a module(9) contained in row 2, named 'M1'. Rows 5, 6 and 7 are its three ports, each a port(10) contained in row 4.

The energy management example uses the same shape with a router that has 16 slots with line cards. The chassis is row 1 with entPhysicalClass chassis(3) and entPhysicalContainedIn 0; the slot is row 2 with class container(5) contained in row 1; and the line card is row 4 with class module(9) contained in row 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is a router with two slots, each holding a three-port module. The chassis is the top row, the slots sit inside it, and the modules sit inside the slots. Each row points to its parent, so a management station can rebuild the whole layout.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of management objects in these MIB modules have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and such objects may be sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. Support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. The RFC names entPhysicalSerialNum, entPhysicalAlias, entPhysicalAssetID and entPhysicalUris. Their misconfiguration or disclosure may reveal sensitive information about assets, perturb the management of entities, or cause privacy issues if they allow tracking of values that are personally identifying.

Readable objects can also be sensitive, so it is important to control even GET or NOTIFY access to them and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network. The RFC lists entPhysicalDescr, entPhysicalVendorType, entPhysicalHardwareRev, entPhysicalFirmwareRev, entPhysicalSoftwareRev, entPhysicalMfgName, entPhysicalModelName and entPhysicalUUID, because they expose the vendor, model, version and specific device identification of each system component. entLogicalDescr and entLogicalType expose the types of logical entities present, entLogicalCommunity exposes community names, entLogicalTAddress and entLogicalTDomain expose network addresses, and entLogicalContextEngineID and entLogicalContextName identify the authoritative SNMP engine.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Even if the network itself is secure, there is no control over who may access and GET or SET the objects in these MIB modules. Implementations SHOULD provide the security features described by the SNMPv3 framework, and implementations claiming compliance with SNMPv3 MUST include full support for authentication and privacy via the User-based Security Model with the AES cipher algorithm. Deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. The RFC recommends deploying SNMPv3 with cryptographic security enabled, and making it the operator's responsibility to configure the SNMP entity so that only principals with legitimate rights can read or change these objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these objects reveal serial numbers, asset tags, model names and network addresses, and a few of them can be written. The document says the safe way to use them is SNMPv3, which authenticates and encrypts the traffic, and it says older SNMP versions should not be deployed.

viz.caption: THE FIVE OBJECT GROUPS IN THE ENTITY MIB

items.title: entityPhysical
items.text: One table with a row per physical component.

items.title: entityLogical
items.text: One row per logical entity, such as a router or a bridge.

items.title: entityMapping
items.text: Links physical components to logical entities, interfaces and ports.

items.title: entityGeneral
items.text: General attributes shared by all entity types; now a single object, entLastChangeTime.

items.title: entityNotifications
items.text: Notifications that report the status of the MIB instance.

viz.caption: IANAPHYSICALCLASS VALUES FOR THE CLASS OF A COMPONENT

items.label: other
items.desc: The class is known but matches no supported value.

items.label: unknown
items.desc: The class is unknown to the agent.

items.label: chassis
items.desc: An overall container for networking equipment.

items.label: backplane
items.desc: A device that aggregates and forwards traffic, such as a shared backplane.

items.label: container
items.desc: Holds one or more removable entities, such as a chassis slot.

items.label: fan
items.desc: A fan or other heat-reduction component.

items.label: sensor
items.desc: A sensor, such as a temperature sensor within a router chassis.

items.label: module
items.desc: A self-contained sub-system, such as a plug-in card or daughter-card.

items.label: port
items.desc: A networking port that receives or transmits traffic.

items.label: stack
items.desc: A super-container that groups multiple chassis entities.

items.label: energyObject
items.desc: Equipment monitored or controlled for energy management.
